own_scenes.desc: El punk empieza en Inglaterra en 1975-76 y llega a California cuatro años después; de él sale el hardcore, fuerte en ambas costas estadounidenses y muy parecido al thrash naciente. Su código es el contrario del heavy: cualquiera puede tocar, voz plana sin emoción, igualdad entre fans y músicos frente a los guitar heroes. Grupos como los Misfits, llamados indistintamente horror metal y horror punk, muestran que la mezcla es posible; el thrash será un bricolage de segundo orden entre ambos códigos contradictorios.

refs.q: This emphasis on skill contrasts with the punk code, which emphasizes the simplicity of playing
refs.para: The style of play owes much to blues-based guitarists who transformed the urban blues–guitar sound into rock. Following the blues-rock tradition, heavy metal guitarists are required to demonstrate technical proficiency. This emphasis on skill contrasts with the punk code, which emphasizes the simplicity of playing, the idea that “hey, anybody can do this, I just learned it two weeks ago.” Punk stresses a leveling between fans and performers; heavy metal, with its guitar heroes, emphasizes distance.
refs.chapter: Cap. 2: Heavy metal: la bestia que se niega a morir

refs.q: Groups such as the Misfits, which was alternately called a horror-metal band and a horror-punk band, showed the possibilities for a blending of punk and metal.
refs.para: Speed/thrash was most directly influenced by NWOBHM groups, such as Venom, Diamond Head, and Iron Maiden, all of which made rhythmic innovations. But it also followed in a line already present in heavy metal’s golden age. Moreover, speed/thrash bears the trace of the punk explosion. Punk began in England in 1975–76 and reached California four years later. It spawned hardcore, which was particularly strong on both coasts of the United States and bore many resemblances to the erupting speed/thrash style. Groups such as the Misfits, which was alternately called a horror-metal band and a horror-punk band, showed the possibilities for a blending of punk and metal. A more direct influence of hardcore entered the subgenre beginning in 1985–86, when groups such as DRI (Dirty Rotten Imbeciles) and Suicidal Tendencies created a style within a style, termed “thrashcore” or “crossover.”⁶⁶ Its traces reinforced the punk-related elements that were already present in the subgenre.

own_scenes.place: Essex y el sureste de Inglaterra
own_scenes.desc: N-Joi (RCA, 1991) mezcló techno con montones de breakbeats sampleados («Let the bass kick», «Drop the bass now!») y entró en el terreno fronterizo con el hip hop que se llamó hardcore. Liam Howlett, antiguo DJ de «brit-hop», unió el breakbeat al house rápido; con What Evil Lurks (1990) fichó por XL con Leeroy Thornhill y el bailarín Keith Flint, y «Charly» fue número tres británico en 1991. Los ravers vieron en sus ritmos dispersos (y en sus muchos clones infantiles) un anatema contra el bombo a negras; Mixmag preguntó en portada en 1992: «¿Mató “Charly” al rave?». De esa división nacieron el jungle y el drum & bass. Prodigy triunfó en Estados Unidos con estética punk y Flint como cantante, en el sello Maverick de Madonna: The Fat of the Land (1997), con «Firestarter» y «Breathe», más de dos millones de copias.

refs.q: The U.K. dance music magazine Mixmag even went as far as asking the following on a 1992 cover: “Did ‘Charly’ Kill Rave?”
refs.para: The Prodigy’s founder, Liam Howlett, like so many other English techno and acid house fans of the early 1990s, was grounded in the fundamentals of hip-hop. As a former “brit-hop” DJ himself, it was natural that Howlett would begin joining the breakbeat to up-tempo house music in his own compositions. What Evil Lurks, released in 1990, got the group’s trio (Howlett, Leeroy Thornhill, and dancer Keith Flint) signed to XL Records, a U.K. label. The Prodigy’s second single, “Charly,” was its watershed moment, codifying its breakbeat approach and scoring a No. 1 hit on the U.K. National Dance Chart and a No. 3 slot on the U.K. Gallup Top 40 in 1991. But success came at a small price—ravers initially judged the scattershot rhythms of “breakbeat house” (and the many juvenile “Charly” clones) as anathema to the steady four-count bliss they had enjoyed since 1988’s “Summer of Love.” The U.K. dance music magazine Mixmag even went as far as asking the following on a 1992 cover: “Did ‘Charly’ Kill Rave?”

own_scenes.desc: El punk como «violento, rápido y ruidoso» tarda en conquistar EE UU, pero cuando lo hace el hardcore se convierte durante dos décadas en el idioma nacional de millones de chavales. Misfits y el «scum-rock»; el crossover punk-metal (Suicidal Tendencies, Corrosion Of Conformity, Agnostic Front); Mission Of Burma en Boston. Washington: Bad Brains (reggae, funk y metal diez años por delante), Minor Threat (el «straight-edge») y Rites Of Spring, inventores del emo-core. San Francisco: Dead Kennedys de Jello Biafra, D.R.I. (thrash antes que Metallica), Flipper. Los «beach punks» de Los Ángeles: Germs, X, Black Flag (Damaged), Descendents, Gun Club (Fire Of Love), Bad Religion. El jazz-core de Minutemen y Saccharine Trust; en el Medio Oeste, Husker Du y Replacements cambian el hardcore para siempre; en Chicago, Naked Raygun y Big Black de Steve Albini; en Europa, The Ex y los italianos CCCP.

notes.text: Beltram es la punta de una escuela de Brooklyn (Tommy Musto, Frankie Bones, Lenny Dee), ex b-boys más interesados en la energía del hip hop que en la emoción de Detroit. En Frankfurt, el colectivo PCP de Marc Acardipane practica electrónica extrema, casi industrial.

refs.q: Beltram no fue un caso aislado, sino la punta del iceberg de una nueva escuela de productores en la Gran Manzana
refs.para: El de Queens fue, pues, el responsable de la reputación que alcanzó R&S en los primeros noventa como uno de los sellos más ruidosos del planeta, responsable de discos que, como decía John McReady en su A-Z Of Techno, «suenan como toda una calle llena de coches a los que se les ha disparado la alarma». Pero Beltram no fue un caso aislado, sino la punta del iceberg de una nueva escuela de productores en la Gran Manzana, la mayoría de ellos concentrada en Brooklyn, que respondían a nombres tan neoyorquinos como Tommy Musto, Lenny Dee o Frankie «Bones». Eran jóvenes y estaban dispuestos a comerse el mundo, a romper las barreras que separaban house y techno, mas interesados en la energía y agresividad del hip hop —casi todos eran ex b-boys— que en la emoción del techno de Detroit. Ellos convirtieron el sampler en su arma predilecta para crear nuevos y fantasiosos híbridos: el tándem Musto-Bones ensayó su improbable mezcla de techno, house, hip hop y lo que se les pusiera a tiro para crear un nuevo tipo de freestyle urbano en su aclamada serie Looney Tunes o en los incombustibles maxis Bonesbreaks. Nació así una concepción típicamente made in New York del techno que tuvo, con marcados altibajos, continuidad durante toda la década.

similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: Mientras las revistas anuncian la «muerte del punk», el hardcore se convierte en un movimiento que no deja pueblo sin tocar y genera subgéneros. El «emocore» (Jawbreaker, Weezer, Sunny Day Real Estate, Promise Ring, At The Drive-In, Jimmy Eat World, Seaweed); el hardcore progresivo de Washington (Nation Of Ulysses, Make-Up, Shudder To Think, Jawbox, Edsel, Lungfish, Circus Lupus, Dismemberment Plan); el «ska-core» (Operation Ivy, Rancid, Mighty Mighty Bosstones, Sublime, No Doubt); el punk-pop que llega a las listas (Green Day, Offspring, Flop, Pennywise, Pegboy, Superchunk, Queers); el garage-punk californiano (Drive Like Jehu, Rocket From The Crypt, Blink 182, Zen Guerrilla); el jazzcore (Bazooka, Iceburn); la vieja escuela (D Generation, Supersuckers, Zeke, Dropkick Murphys, Silverfish, Turbonegro) y el post-hardcore de Unwound.

similar_scenes.desc: Hacia 1990 la música rave acelera hasta 150 bpm: breaks hiperactivos, voces aceleradas, riffs de piano caricaturescos. Para Simon Reynolds, fruto del aumento de las dosis de éxtasis. Mezcla de new beat, Detroit duro, breakbeats acelerados, riffs industriales como «Energy Flash» y melodías de dibujos animados. Del hardcore sale el germen del jungle y buena parte de la dance music de los noventa.

podcast.title: Emergence from Rave Scene Fragmentation (1993)
podcast.body: Hardcore emerged around 1993 as the increasingly vast rave scene began to fracture. New subcultures within the movement demanded faster, harder, and more radical sounds, leading to the development of hardcore as a distinct and diverse branch of rave music. "De esta expresión surgió lo que pronto se conocería como hardcore, la Rave dungra narbol del que blotaría ambaya ramas diferentes."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Qué fue el GABBER y por qué asustaba a Europa

podcast.title: "Damaged" as an Introduction
podcast.body: For Nate Mendel, the Black Flag album "Damaged" served as a crucial entry point into understanding hardcore music. The album's "energy," "aggression," and "weirdness" resonated with him, defining what the genre was about. "Well, the one that, that, where I understood what hardcore we call it, hardcore at the time was about, was, uh, black flags damaged."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 80s Concept Album Example
podcast.body: Hüsker Dü released a breakthrough hardcore album in the 1980s that also functioned as a concept album, marking an early instance of the format within the alt rock lineage. "before we moved on to a breakthrough hardcore album from Husker Doe in the 1980s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Aggressive Dance Forms (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: Hardcore emerged from punk rock in the late 1970s as one of the most aggressive forms of music. This genre encouraged dancing with "enthusiasm," which involved deliberately crashing or slamming into other dancers, giving rise to "slam dancing." "This was among the most aggressive forms of music ever invented. The idea was to dance with, well, let's call it enthusiasm, deliberately crashing or slamming into other dancers, hence the term slam dancing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Aggressive Turn in North America (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: In North America, music had turned aggressive in some quarters, including hardcore, indicating early shifts. "And dust-trimon music and hardcore, for example."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: American Invention and Characteristics
podcast.body: Hardcore punk was an American invention, predominantly from the West Coast, that intensified the original punk rock formula. It became faster, more aggressive, harsher, angrier, and more violent, characterized by a high "testosterone" level. It vehemently opposed the status quo, mainstream rock, and corporate culture, positioning itself as intensely anti-rock star. "Hardcore is against anything that the status quo had to offer. It had to be as far from mainstream rock as possible."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: American Invention and Evolution
podcast.body: Hardcore emerged as an American invention, serving as a direct descendant of the hard, fast, and loud punk music of the 1970s. It sought to amplify these characteristics, making the music even harder, faster, and louder than its predecessor, though bands still occasionally yielded to the temptation to sing "fun songs" amidst the genre's intensity. "The direct descendants of the hard, fast, and loud punk of the 1970s was hardcore, an American invention that tried to amp things up so that the music was even harder, faster, and louder than punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bay Area Hardcore (San Francisco)
podcast.body: Despite San Francisco's hippie history, or perhaps because of it, the Bay Area became a significant magnet for hardcore punk bands, with Dead Kennedys being particularly important. "Although the place had a hippie history, or maybe because of it, the Bay Area became a magnet for hardcore punk bands, and no other band was more important than the dead Kennedys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Boston Hardcore Scene and "The Boston Crew"
podcast.body: Boston's hardcore scene included bands influenced by Ian MacKaye's straight edge philosophy. The "Boston Crew" were self-appointed "moral police" who would often physically confront anyone seen drinking or doing drugs at shows, creating an intense atmosphere. "Some of these bands were influenced by Ian McKay's straight edge philosophy. They were so intense that the straight edge guys would often brawl with anyone they saw drinking or doing drugs at their shows. Those self-affointed more police were locally known as the Boston Crow."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: California as Hardcore Center
podcast.body: California, particularly Los Angeles and Orange County, served as a central hub for hardcore culture, fostering numerous influential bands in the main cities and surrounding suburbs. "California was the center of hardcore culture with so many bands, an LA and Orange County and the suburbs to the North, the Minutemen, the descendants, Agent Orange, the adolescents, social distortion, Red Cross."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Canadian Hardcore Scenes
podcast.body: Canada had several important hardcore bands beyond D.O.A., with notable scenes in Toronto (e.g., Fucked Up from Kensington Market), Montreal (The Asexuals), Edmonton (SNFU), and particularly the West Coast (e.g., The Subhumans, Dayglo Abortions, NoMeansNo). "Canada wasn't immune. We've already talked about DOA, but they were far from the only important hardcore band from Canada. In Toronto, there was a bunch of effing goofs who came out of the Kensington Market neighborhood. Montreal gave us the asexuals. SNFU came from Edmonton. But the West Coast had the most fertile ground, the subhumans and dayglow abortions, for example."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Catalyst for Alternative Music
podcast.body: Hardcore was instrumental in establishing the concept of alternative music in the early and mid-1980s. This movement eventually led major labels to sign influential bands who, in turn, shaped subsequent generations of music. "Hardcore helped create the whole notion of alternative music in early and middle 1980s, eventually leading major labels to some great bands who in turn influenced the next generation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Contemporary Revival
podcast.body: The genre of hardcore is experiencing a renewed interest, with new DJs actively blending classic sounds with current trends. This resurgence is evident in the revival of major events like Thunderdome and the emergence of new large-scale hardcore festivals. "se ha despertado un interés renovado en la música hardcore, con nuevos DJs que mezclan sonidos clásicos contendencias actuales."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Qué fue el GABBER y por qué asustaba a Europa

podcast.title: Continued Global Presence
podcast.body: Hardcore continues to thrive globally today, manifesting in a diverse range of sounds and styles, exemplified by modern bands like Baltimore's Turnstile, who blend hardcore roots with experimental directions. "And hardcore lives today around the world in a variety of sounds and flavors. For example, there's Baltimore's Turn Style, a group with serious hardcore roots or taking things in a more experimental direction."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dead Kennedys' Contribution
podcast.body: The highly political Bay Area punk band, The Dead Kennedys, played a significant role in establishing the stylistic foundation for what would later be known as Hardcore music. "The highly political Dead Kennedys, a Bay Area punk band that helps at the table for what would later be called Hardcore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Definition and Grievances
podcast.body: Hardcore punk, or hardcore, is a subgenre of punk rock. Its creators were drawn to the faster and heavier aspects of original punk bands and sought to express grievances against societal norms. These grievances included disgust with yuppies and their culture, broken homes, ruined families, capitalist exploitation, consumerism, and corrupt politicians. They also disliked "high and mighty rock stars," New Wave aesthetics (skinny ties, eyeliner), and the established music industry, sometimes just wanting to "get wasted." "Hardcore punk, or just hardcore, if you prefer, is a subgenre, obviously, of punk rock. Its creators love the faster and heavier end of the original punk rock bands, but they also had, well, they had some grievances that they needed to express. Epis and their culture disgusted them, broken homes and ruined families, destroyed them, capitalist exploitation, yuppies, consumerism, corrupt politicians. They also aren't crazy about high and muddy rock stars, or the posters of New Wave with their skinny ties and eyeliner, the weasels of the established recorded music industry, and sometimes the people behind Hardcore just wanted to get wasted."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Diversity in Contributors
podcast.body: While hardcore was largely composed of white males, some of its most important contributors were Black and Latino, highlighting the genre's internal diversity despite its typical demographic profile. "Hardcore was largely made up of white males, but some of the sounds most important contributors were black and Latino."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early 1990s Influence - Mia Zapata
podcast.body: Mia Zapata is considered a significant influence on the hardcore scene of the early 1990s. "If you're into hardcore or the ride girl scene of the early 1990s you may have, she was in a band called The Gits. She's considered to be a big influence on a lot of the women attached to and inspired by this scene."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Reach to Japan
podcast.body: Hardcore reached Japan surprisingly early, establishing a scene there as far back as 1977. "It even reached Japan as early as 1977."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early West Coast Sound
podcast.body: In Los Angeles and Southern California, the original punk rock scene had faded by 1979, replaced by a new, even more stripped-down type of punk. This sound typically featured guitars, bass, drums, and a vocalist, with traditional verse-chorus structures often abandoned in favor of extremely short songs, sometimes under 32 seconds. "The original punk rock scene was gone by about 1979, and in its place was a new type of punk that was stripped down even further. Guitar's bass drums vocalist, that's it. The traditional first chorus first song structure wasn't necessary. In fact, if everything could be said in 32 seconds or less, so be it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Economics of Indie Bands
podcast.body: For bands like Husker Dü, the economics of being an indie hardcore band became unsustainable, prompting them to sign with major labels to ensure a longer career, reliable payment, downtime, and wider audience reach. "The economics of being an indie band just didn't work for them anymore. They couldn't afford to stay indie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 1

podcast.title: Essential for Grunge
podcast.body: Hardcore's influence was so profound that it is considered essential to the emergence of grunge, implying that without hardcore, grunge would not have developed as it did. "Honestly, no hardcore, no grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Foundational Genre
podcast.body: Hardcore was a foundational genre for Alexis on Fire, from which their sound evolved. The band members "came up through Hardcore and punk rock," viewing their music as the next natural progression. "We all kind of came up, I think, through Hardcore and punk rock and stuff like that. And this was just the next progression of that, you know?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alexisonfire - In Their Own Words Podcast

podcast.title: Fusion with Ska
podcast.body: A segment of the American punk underground fused Ska with hardcore influences, playing a significant role in the development of the third wave of Ska in the early 1990s. "Given their background they inevitably fused SCAT with hardcore influences."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Geographic Origins and Spread (Late 1970s)
podcast.body: Hardcore first took root simultaneously on both the East and West Coasts of North America in the late 1970s, specifically in Vancouver, San Francisco, Southern California, Washington, D.C., Boston, and New York City. From these North American scenes, it spread to the UK, Italy, and Japan. "Hardcore first took root on the East and West Coast of North America in the late 1970s, specifically in Vancouver, San Francisco, Southern California, Washington, D.C., Boston, and New York City. The UK also had its own Hardcore scenes, and from there it spread to Italy and Japan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Gospel Spread by Touring
podcast.body: Hardcore bands like Black Flag and Bad Religion were known for spreading the "gospel of hardcore" by touring constantly, establishing a strong underground presence and influence. "And there were bands like Black Flag and Bad Religion that spread the gospel of hardcore by touring constantly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hardcore in Eastern Europe
podcast.body: Before the fall of the Iron Curtain, hardcore was a potent underground force in Eastern Europe, demonstrating its ability to thrive in politically restrictive environments. "Hardcore was a powerful underground force in Eastern Europe before the fall of the Iron Curtain."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hüsker Dü's Impact
podcast.body: Hüsker Dü made a major impact in American hardcore by blending the genre's power and energy with melody and more conventional song structures, sometimes even incorporating piano and acoustic guitars. "In the history of American hardcore, they were a major influence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact of Rocky Mountains on West Coast Touring
podcast.body: The presence of the Rocky Mountains made touring north-south along the West Coast (from San Diego to Vancouver) much easier and more affordable for bands than touring east-west across North America. This geographic reality fostered a semi-distinct ecosystem for West Coast bands and influenced the spread of hardcore. "If you're in a band on the west coast, it is much easier and much more affordable to tour north south than it is east west. You can blame the Rocky Mountains. It takes time to cross the range and there aren't that many places to play between the western and eastern slopes. So that means for a certain level of band, you inhabit a semi distinct ecosystem. You're not cut off from the rest of the continent, but it does affect how you tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Other Genres
podcast.body: Hardcore has had a significant and undeniable influence on various other music forms, including metal, post-hardcore, skate punk, emo, Riot Grrrl, and grunge. "First of all, we've seen the influence this music has had on metal and in creating post-hardcore music as well as skate punk and emo. Metal, emo, riot girls, grunge is undeniable."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Thrash Metal
podcast.body: Hardcore punk began to influence metal bands, pushing them to play faster and harder. This fusion ultimately led to the creation and development of the thrash metal genre. "Hardcore punk began to influence metal. Metal bands started playing faster and harder, resulting in thrash metal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: International Expansion in the 1980s
podcast.body: Hardcore punk rapidly spread globally in the 1980s, driven by bands relentlessly touring and playing inexpensive all-ages shows in towns and cities that mainstream acts often overlooked. This allowed kids seeking a musical scene to connect with the genre. "It's amazing the number of places where hardcore punk caught on during the 1980s. And then again, maybe not because all these bands toured relentlessly, often playing inexpensive all-ager shows and towns and cities with kids who wanted to belong to some kind of musical scene, but had been left behind by the Bigger Acts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Male-Centric Evolution
podcast.body: While original punk aimed for equal opportunity, a significant offshoot called hardcore, an American-bred ultra-intense form of punk that took root in the 1980s, became very male-centric. This genre, powered by testosterone, often featured rough and violent gigs and was generally unwelcoming to women. "Hardcore, the American bread ultra-intense offshoot of punk that took root in the 1980s was powered by pure testosterone. Gigs could get very rough and very violent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Women Who Rocked The 90's

podcast.title: Midwest Hardcore Hub: Minneapolis
podcast.body: Minneapolis in the Midwest was a crucial hub for hardcore, producing highly influential bands like The Replacements and Hüsker Dü, who later became significant forces in alt-rock. "There were other American cities that got cut up in hardcore, Detroit, Phoenix, various spots in Texas, North Carolina, Chicago, and maybe most importantly in the Midwest Minneapolis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Characteristics
podcast.body: The aim of hardcore was to play harder, faster, and louder than anyone else. Technical skill and virtuosity were only valued if they contributed to this goal. Melody was often considered "wimpy," with shouting and screaming deemed more important for vocal delivery. "The aim was to play harder, faster, and louder than everyone else. Technique and virtuosity? Only if it helped you play harder, faster, and louder. Melody? Eh, wimpy. Shouting and screaming was more important."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New York Hardcore Scene Characteristics
podcast.body: The hardcore music in New York City had a distinct sound, sometimes referred to as the "New York Hardcore sound." This scene was home to early Beastie Boys, Agnostic Front, Cro-Mags, and the Misfits. "From DC, we head to New York City. The music was a little different too. Some people called this the New York Hardcore Tug."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Political Engagement
podcast.body: Hardcore inspired people across the political spectrum to engage in politics, fostering activism in places like the Middle East and Indonesia, where Muslim hardcore acts used the genre to protest human rights injustices. "People got into politics because of hardcore, and we're talking all sides of the political spectrum. This includes Muslim hardcore acts in places like the Middle East and Indonesia, who used this style of music to rail against human rights and justices."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Punk Subgenre
podcast.body: Hardcore emerged as one of the sub-genres into which punk rock mutated as it receded from the mainstream in the 1980s, preserving the punk attitude and DIY tenets. "It mutated into sub-genres like hardcore and oi and a narco punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reagan Era Rebellion and Community
podcast.body: American Hardcore flourished during the Reagan years, serving as a broad rebellion against everything, including the perceived rebellion of the original punk rockers. Despite its rebellious nature, it fostered a strong community through fanzines, dedicated promoters, and collaborative projects, such as the formation of independent record labels specifically for hardcore acts. "American Hardcore rose during the Reagan years, and was all about rebelling against, well, everything, including the rebellion of the original punk rockers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: Shared Influence for Ho99o9
podcast.body: The members of Ho99o9, TheOGM and Yeti999, bonded over their shared love for hardcore music, alongside hip-hop and horror movies, which influenced the formation of their punk rap group. "They both loved hardcore and they loved hip-hop."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Straight Edge Lifestyle
podcast.body: This is a specific hardcore lifestyle adopted by bands like Hard Stance, characterized by strict adherence to abstinence from alcohol, recreational drugs, and even cigarettes. "This meant no drinking, no drugs, not even cigarettes ever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Touring Underserved Cities
podcast.body: The north-south touring flow of punk and hardcore bands meant they frequently played in underserved cities and towns, including the Seattle area, where major touring acts were infrequent. This created opportunities for local scenes to flourish and for unique cross-pollination of musical styles. "The North South flow of punk and hardcore bands meant that these groups played a lot of underserved cities and towns when it came to tours. They had to play somewhere so they would play anywhere. And that included the Seattle area. At the time, the Pacific Northwest was sort of off the grid when it came to major touring acts. So if you wanted to see live music, it was much easier to catch a punk show than anything else."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: UK Hardcore and D-Beat
podcast.body: The UK developed its own hardcore derivative called D-Beat, characterized by a distinctive drum pattern. UK Hardcore was a fusion of British punk (like the Sex Pistols) and the New Wave of British Heavy Metal (NWOBHM) bands that emerged in the early 1980s, with Motörhead being a major influence. "Then we have the UK, home of a hardcore derivative called Debeat, which referred to a distinctive sort of drum pattern that went with a lot of the songs. UK Hardcore was an amalgamation of British punk, especially the Sex Bistels, and the new wave of British heavy metal bands that appeared at the beginning of the 1980s. The biggest influence from that scene was Motorhead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Vancouver's Historic Scene
podcast.body: In the 1970s and 1980s, Vancouver was predominantly known for its hardcore music scene. Bands like No Means No, DOA, and Adversity emerged from this era, contributing to the city's distinctive and influential musical "edge" that Matthew Good believes has since been lost. "If you look at the city's music history, I mean, we're predominantly known for hardcore in the 80s and the 70s, 80s, that kind of thing."
